clue.text: Back in olden times, Corinthians added fishy oil to greens

indicators.note: going back means the Corinthians abbreviation is read from its end to its start
one piece sits inside the abbreviation for the era of olden times
something fishy is suspect and not as it should be, so the letters of oil are jumbled

blocks.note: BC, before Christ, marks dates in ancient times
Cor is the standard abbreviation for the Bible book Corinthians
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A recipe from antiquity: the Corinthians dressing their vegetables with fish oil.
explanation.walkthrough: BC, before Christ, is the usual crossword shorthand for olden times, and Cor is how Bible references abbreviate Corinthians.
explanation.definitionFit: Broccoli is a green vegetable, and greens is the everyday plural for such leafy vegetables.

clue.text: Disagree with Post Offices breaking public contract

indicators.note: something breaking into a word splits it open and sits in the middle
to contract is to shrink, so the word for public loses its last letter

blocks.note: something public is open to all
PO is the abbreviation for a post office, made plural

explanation.surface: Someone objects to post office branches walking away from a public service agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a noun, a legal agreement, but it is a verb telling you to shorten a word by its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To oppose something is to be against it, a verb meaning the same as disagreeing with it.

clue.text: Royal wine merchants?

blocks.note: first meaning: kingly, stately and grand
second meaning: ... Wine, a British chain of wine shops

explanation.surface: A question about who supplies the palace cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: Majestic Wine is a well-known chain of wine retailers in Britain; the question mark flags the proper-noun meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes regal grandeur fit for a monarch, and it is also the trading name of a British wine retailer.

clue.text: Flier using thermals gets good cover above East River

indicators.note: in a down entry, one part placed above another simply comes first in the reading

blocks.note: G is a standard abbreviation for good
a lid covers a container
compass abbreviation
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A pilot riding warm air currents finds good cloud cover over an eastern river.
explanation.definitionFit: A glider is an engineless aircraft that stays aloft by riding rising currents of warm air.

clue.text: Good man's ready behind bar

indicators.note: one part coming behind another means it follows it in the reading order

blocks.note: a good man is a saint, abbreviated St
fruit that is ready to eat is ripe

explanation.surface: A decent fellow is all set and waiting behind the pub counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, but it is the definition in its sense of a band or line.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripe is a long narrow band of colour, which is one sense of a bar, as in a bar of colour on a flag.

clue.text: Spade thus overtakes hearts and victory with one point left

indicators.note: read as 'takes over', one word wraps itself round and takes in another

blocks.note: so means in this way
H is the card-suit abbreviation for hearts
V for victory
a compass point, here east
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A bridge or whist game: spades beat hearts and win the hand with a point to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-game picture of spades and hearts is a decoy: Spade is the definition, a digging tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A shovel and a spade are both long-handled digging tools, close enough to be synonyms.

clue.text: Strike legislation is about to get chop

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word for legislation is read backwards

blocks.note: legislation is the making of law
to lop is to chop off

explanation.surface: A new law is about to be axed, the way bad bills often are.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallop is a heavy blow, and as a verb it means to hit hard, a synonym of strike.

clue.text: Little bird's in wee box

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one word is shut inside another

blocks.note: wee and pee are both informal words for urine
a tit is a small songbird

explanation.surface: A small bird has got itself into a tiny box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' looks like Scots for small, chiming with Little, but it is the other wee, giving PEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Petite means small and dainty, an adjective like little, usually said of a woman's build.

clue.text: Cook's sending a boy up to ask about dessert

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up means reading it from bottom to top
about here means moved around, so the letters of the word ask are jumbled

blocks.note: to bake is to cook in an oven; the 's reads as 'is'
a boy is a lad
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A chef sends a lad upstairs to find out about the pudding order.
explanation.walkthrough: BAKE plus A LAD turned upwards gives BAKEDALA, and a jumbled ASK supplies SKA.
explanation.definitionFit: Baked Alaska is a pudding of sponge and ice cream encased in meringue and briefly browned in a hot oven.

clue.text: No cop can be hot in a cape!

indicators.note: what letters can be is what they can be turned into, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the tap abbreviation for hot

explanation.surface: A superhero joke: no policeman can stay cool when wearing a cape.
explanation.definitionFit: A poncho is a blanket-like outer garment with a hole for the head, a kind of cape.

clue.text: Story of an East London love

blocks.note: taken as written
EC, East Central, is the postcode area for the City of London
to dote on someone is to love them fondly

explanation.surface: A tale of a romance in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: London postcodes begin with district letters, and EC covers the eastern central part of the city.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a short personal story, usually told in conversation, so it is one kind of story.

clue.text: Cast vote to reject a proposal

indicators.note: something cast is thrown or moulded into a new shape, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A committee member casts a ballot to throw out a motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast vote' is the natural phrase for using a ballot, which hides 'Cast' as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To veto is to use a right of refusal to block a measure, a verb meaning to reject what is put forward.

clue.text: Even well-fed Conservative has to respect voters

indicators.note: even means the second, fourth and sixth letters, the even-numbered ones, are kept

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of the hyphenated word
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written
to rate someone is to think highly of them

explanation.surface: Even a comfortable, well-off Tory politician must respect the people who vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' reads as 'even so', but it picks letters 2, 4 and 6 of well-fed.
explanation.definitionFit: The electorate is the whole body of people entitled to vote in an election, so it means the voters collectively.

clue.text: Flyover etiquette in guide for road users?

blocks.note: a flyover is literally a road raised high, a high way
etiquette is a code of manners

explanation.surface: A question about how drivers should behave on an elevated road, as set out for motorists.
explanation.walkthrough: The Highway Code is the official British rulebook for drivers, cyclists and pedestrians; 'Flyover' splits as a road up high.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highway Code is the official UK government handbook of rules and advice that all road users are expected to follow.

clue.text: Chaps restrain a rampant rogue being a pain

indicators.note: rampant means rearing up on hind legs, so in a down entry the word for rogue runs upwards
to restrain is to hold in, so the chaps hold the other letters between them

blocks.note: a chap is a he, and two of them make chaps
taken as written
a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue

explanation.surface: Some men hold back an unruly scoundrel who is making a nuisance of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Plural chaps give two HEs, one either side of A and an upturned CAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A headache is an ache in the head, and figuratively a nuisance, so either sense can stand for a pain.

clue.text: Issued GI going abroad with camouflage

indicators.note: abroad here means scattered widely, so the letters spread out and settle in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An American soldier posted overseas is handed his camouflage kit.
explanation.walkthrough: A GI is an American soldier; the military picture makes 'going abroad' look like a posting.
explanation.definitionFit: Camouflage and disguise both mean concealing appearance so as not to be recognised or noticed.

clue.text: Annoy right away, getting son to make joints

indicators.note: right sent away means the letter standing for right is removed from the word

blocks.note: to rankle is to annoy or irritate
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Someone irritates people at once, and gets their son to make the joint for dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: The ankle is the hinge where the foot meets the leg, one of the body's joints.

clue.text: Flower child's immersed in love and free

indicators.note: something immersed is plunged inside, so the child abbreviation goes within other letters

blocks.note: love is nil in tennis, the shape of O
to rid is to free of something
CH is a standard abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: A hippie-era flower child is wrapped up in free love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower child' reads as one phrase about hippies, but it splits: Flower is the definition and child the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchid is an exotic plant prized for its showy blooms, an example of a flower.

clue.text: Annual pest problem is disgusting

indicators.note: a problem is something wrong, so the letters are in a troubled order needing sorting

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that the yearly infestation of bugs is revolting.
explanation.definitionFit: Unpleasant and disgusting are both adjectives for something offensive or nasty, the second a stronger form.

clue.text: Kitty's friend set up computer

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting something up makes it read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a kitty is a pot of pooled money
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A cat's companion has configured a PC.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' looks like a cat, but it is the shared pot of money people chip into.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable computer small enough to rest on your knees.

clue.text: Works out total for two drinks

blocks.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits, and a sup is a sip

explanation.surface: Someone tallies the bill for a round of two drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The two drinks are a tot, a small measure of spirits, and a sup, a mouthful.
explanation.definitionFit: To tot up is a British phrasal verb meaning to add numbers together to reach a sum.

clue.text: Hard to leave county and old address

indicators.note: a letter leaving a word is taken out of it

blocks.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
a shire is an English county

explanation.surface: Someone finds it hard to move out of the county and their former home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old address' looks like a former home, but it is a form of address, a way of speaking to a king.
explanation.definitionFit: Sire was once the respectful way to speak to a king or lord, so it is an archaic form of address.

clue.text: Fellow sailor takes drink aboard for bar

indicators.note: taking something aboard means carrying it inside, so the drink goes into the other letters

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow
Jack tar, or jack, is an old name for a sailor
to lap is to drink, as a cat does

explanation.surface: A shipmate brings a drink on board to go with a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Fellow and sailor together make F_JACK, which takes LAP in between.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a flapjack is a chewy oat and syrup slice cut into bars, so it is a kind of bar.

clue.text: Enlightened, thanks to reformed thug

indicators.note: reformed means formed again in a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has seen the light thanks to a thug who has mended his ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Taught is the past form of teach, and to enlighten someone is to teach them, so both mean instructed.

clue.text: Provide calming influence so others are content

indicators.note: read as a noun, content means what is held inside the words before it

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Be a soothing presence so that everyone around you is happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy, the natural end of the sentence, but it is the noun: the contents of so others.
explanation.definitionFit: To soothe is to calm or comfort, so it is a verb meaning to provide a calming influence.

clue.text: Carried on with FBI agent guarding American warship

indicators.note: to guard something is to surround it protectively, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a fed is American slang for a federal agent
USS, United States Ship, prefixes US Navy vessel names

explanation.surface: Someone continued their work alongside a federal agent protecting a navy vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried on' looks like 'continued', but it is the British sense of making a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain, to carry on is to make a scene or complain loudly, the same as having fussed.
